newsitem.title: FRANCE: French voters raise possibility of "cohabitation".
newsitem.headline: French voters raise possibility of "cohabitation".

text.p: French voters are threatening to force conservative President Jacques Chirac to share power with a left-wing government, an institutional straitjacket he once said "sends shivers down my spine".

France's Socialist-led opposition scored an upset by winning most votes in Sundays first round of the National Assembly election and polling institutes projected it might scoop a majority of seats after runoffs on June 1.

A left-wing win would usher in France's third, and potentially longest, "cohabitation" by forcing Chirac to share power with the left, conceivably until 2002. Late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand cohabited with the right twice, in 1986-88 and 1993-95.
"Like cats we sleep with one eye open," Mitterrand remarked of his uneasy 1986-88 dual act with Chirac, who was prime minister.
In the words of former president Valery Giscard dEstaing, the French delegation which turned up in Tokyo for a Group of Seven summit of industrialised nations was "like a two-headed monster".

In recent days Chirac, urging voters to re-elect his centre-right allies, told them that France's voice in Europe could be undermined by squabbling between a prime minister and president from opposite ideological camps.

But France's two bouts of "cohabitation" hardly bear out his fears. Overall, foreign policy went smoothly in both periods, especially under the second, so-called "velvet cohabitation" between Mitterrand and prime minister Edouard Balladur.
If any one individual in France has suffered from power-sharing, it is Chirac who, as Mitterrands prime minister, found himself being repeatedly outfoxed.
Two years before he won the presidency in 1995, Chirac said that the thought of cohabiting again "sends shivers down my spine".
Now president, Chirac called the snap election gambling that voters would re-elect the centre-right, ensuring him a friendly majority until his seven-year term ends in 2002.
Chirac said last week that France "will only be able to defend its interests if it is capable of speaking with a single voice, a strong voice."

The phrase echoed Mitterrand, who said of his relationship with Chirac in 1986 on the eve of the Tokyo summit: "Each has his role. They can be complementary, but in the last resort, France must have just a single voice towards the outside world."

That summit ended with a knock-out victory for Mitterrand, who attended the final news conference with other leaders while Chirac was forced to sit in silence alone at the foot of the stage, smoking a cigarette.

Yet former European Commission president Jacques Delors, a French Socialist, recalled that a European leader had come to Mitterrand at a 1988 European summit to gripe about Chirac. "It's the French position," he said Mitterrand snapped back.

Chirac's allies have warned voters that Socialist leader Lionel Jospin has only a lukewarm commitment to European Union integration and a single currency. But analysts doubt his European policies would differ much from Chirac's if elected.

Under the constitution, the president has pre-eminence in foreign affairs and is commander-in-chief of the armed forces. But Jacques Attali, a former Mitterrand adviser, said cohabitation would be extremely ambiguous.

"The rules have not been clarified...with the euro currency, the border between domestic and foreign policy will be different than before, with the role of the government, as compared with that of the president, much greater than before," he said.
After a first cabinet session with Chirac, Mitterrand said: "I felt as if I was surrounded by men of whom 60 per cent hate me and 80 per cent are fighting me. I was alone this morning, very alone."
